quick.summary: Why an estimate can be off by a lot, and the quick check that catches it.
quick.takeaway: Compare your estimate with a number you already trust.

beats.line: My estimate says a million of our users will pay. We only have fifty thousand. Possible?
That question is the check. Does it break a number you know?
I started from everyone in the country.
So check it against numbers you know. Users, visits, past sign ups.
Our paying users cannot be more than all our users.
Is a sanity check really worth the time?
A minute now, or a wrong plan for months.
Find the step that broke it, fix it, then check again.

board.text: find the wrong step, then recheck

beats.line: So I compare it with a number I trust. Starting from the whole country broke it.
Right. And every new answer gets the same check.

quiz.question: Your estimate of how many of today’s users will pay is larger than your total users. What does this tell you?
options: An assumption is wrong and needs redoing
The estimate is ambitious but fine
The market is bigger than you thought
quiz.explanation: An estimate that breaks a known limit means one of its inputs is off.

quiz.question: Comparing an estimate with a number you already trust is a quick way to catch big mistakes.
quiz.explanation: If the estimate breaks a known limit or is far from past results, something in it needs checking.
